title: How to Win a Datathon 101
text:
Part 1: Meet & clean your data · Part 2: Exploratory data analysis (EDA) · Part 3: Data modelling
The (hypothetical) client: the City of Vancouver wants to run a campaign that gets residents and visitors exploring more neighbourhoods, driving foot traffic to local businesses. They want to know which areas to promote, and when.
The data: the City of Vancouver’s Public trees dataset (City of Vancouver Open Data Portal, Open Government Licence – Vancouver).
https://opendata.vancouver.ca/explore/assets/public-trees/export/

How to use this notebook 1. Set up your folders: create a folder called data with two subfolders inside it, raw and processed. Put public-trees.csv inside data/raw (in Colab: click the File icon on the left → right-click → New folder, then upload the file into data/raw). 2. Run each cell in order with Shift + Enter. 3. TRY IT YOURSELF! cells are where you get to practice. They come in three levels: Easy · Medium · Hard. 4. Stuck? Try the hint first, then click Show Solution. There’s often more than one right answer!

import pandas as pd

# Show more columns when we print a table
pd.set_option("display.max_columns", 20)

title: How to Win a Datathon 101
text:
0. Load the data
NOTE: This file uses semicolons (;), not commas, to separate columns. If you forget sep=";", everything ends up squished into one column.

trees = pd.read_csv(..., sep=...)
trees_raw = trees.copy()   # keep an untouched copy, just in case!
trees.head()  # shows the first 5 rows of your dataframe

title: How to Win a Datathon 101
text:
1. Structure
What does one row represent? How large is the dataset?

trees.shape   # (rows, columns)

It looks like one row = one tree… but let’s check. What are the most common “tree” names?

trees["Common name"].value_counts().head(15)

TRY IT YOURSELF! (Easy): Return the single most common tree in Vancouver with its count.
Hint: value_counts() sorts from most to least common. How do you keep just the first row?

# your code here



Show solution

trees["Common name"].value_counts().head(1)
The Kwanzan flowering cherry is the most common tree in Vancouver.

TRY IT YOURSELF! (Medium): How many different kinds of trees (common names) are there?
Hint: Look up the pandas method nunique().

# your code here



Show solution

trees["Common name"].nunique()
Over 1,300! That’s a lot of categories, which is something to keep in mind before making a chart with all of them.

title: How to Win a Datathon 101
text:
2. Relevant variables
Which columns help answer our question?

trees.columns

Decision: we keep the columns about what the tree is, how big it is, and where it is. We drop Geom because it repeats the location in a messier format.
We’ll also rename the columns to short, lowercase names with no spaces, which makes them much easier to type!

trees = trees.rename(columns={
    "Asset ID": "...",
    "Address": "address",
    "Common name": "common_name",
    "Genus name": "...",
    "Species name": "species",
    "Cultivar name": "cultivar",
    "height_(m)": "height_m",
    "diameter_(cm)": "...",
    "Local Area": "neighbourhood",
    "geo_point_2d": "location",
})

trees = trees.drop(columns=["Geom"])
trees.head()

TRY IT YOURSELF (Medium): Return the number of columns we have now.

# your code here



Show solution

trees.shape[1]
We went from 11 to 10 columns: Geom was dropped (and the rest were renamed).

title: How to Win a Datathon 101
text:
3. Missing values
Are there any missing values, and if so, how many?

trees.isna().sum()

Thousands of trees have no neighbourhood. Before deleting them, let’s look at where they are.

trees.loc[trees["neighbourhood"].isna(), "address"].value_counts().head(5)

2000 W Georgia St is the address of Stanley Park’s entrance! Stanley Park isn’t one of the City’s official neighbourhoods, so its trees have NA in its place.
Decision: if we had just deleted missing rows, we’d lose one of Vancouver’s most famous parks. For simplicity and time, we’ll label those trees “Stanley Park” and mark the rest as “Unknown”.

is_stanley = trees[...] == "2000 W GEORGIA ST"
trees.loc[is_stanley, ...] = "Stanley Park"
trees["neighbourhood"] = trees["neighbourhood"].fillna(...)

(trees["neighbourhood"] == "Stanley Park").sum()


Sneaky (hidden) missing values
Pandas only counts real blanks as missing. But missing data can hide behind values like "NONE", "XX", 0 or "Unknown".

print("Cultivar = 'NONE':", (trees["cultivar"] == "NONE").sum())
print("Species  = 'XX':  ", (trees["species"] == "XX").sum())

Decision: we turn these into real missing values (NaN), so pandas treats them correctly. We also drop the few trees with no name at all, since we can’t tell what they are.

trees["cultivar"] = trees["cultivar"].replace("___", pd.NA)
trees["species"] = trees["species"].replace("___", pd.NA)

trees = trees.___(subset=["___"])

trees.___().sum()

TRY IT YOURSELF (Easy): Which column has the most missing values now?
Hint: use .sort_values(ascending=False) as part of your solution.

# your code here



Show solution

trees.isna().sum().sort_values(ascending=False)
cultivar, but that’s fine! The cultivar is a very specific variety name, and we don’t need it to answer our client’s question. Not every missing value needs fixing.

TRY IT YOURSELF (Medium): For trees with an “Unknown” neighbourhood, find the 10 most common addresses and how many trees are at each one.

# your code here



Show solution

trees.loc[trees["neighbourhood"] == "Unknown", "address"].value_counts().head(10)

title: How to Win a Datathon 101
text:
4. Data types
Additional exercises: we won’t have time for these during the workshop. Try them on your own afterwards; hints and solutions are included!
Are numbers, dates and categories stored correctly?

trees.dtypes

Height and diameter are numbers. But location is stored as text, like "49.2556, -123.1758", so we can’t put it on a map yet.
Decision: split it into two numeric columns, lat and lon.

trees = trees.dropna(subset=["location"])   # one tree has no location

lat_lon = trees["location"].str.split(",", expand=True)
trees["lat"] = lat_lon[0].astype(float)
trees["lon"] = lat_lon[1].astype(float)

trees = trees.drop(columns=["location"])
trees[["common_name", "lat", "lon"]].head()

TRY IT YOURSELF (Medium): Check the smallest and largest lat and lon values. Do they look like Vancouver? (Vancouver is at roughly 49.2°N, 123.1°W.)
Hint: Try .describe() on just those two columns.

# your code here



Show solution

trees[["lat", "lon"]].describe()
Latitudes are all around 49.2–49.3 and longitudes around −123.0 to −123.2, so everything is in Vancouver. Sanity-checking ranges like this is a quick way to catch errors (e.g., flipped lat/lon).

title: How to Win a Datathon 101
text:
5. Inconsistencies
Additional exercises: we won’t have time for these during the workshop. Try them on your own afterwards; hints and solutions are included!
Is the same thing written in different ways? Are there duplicates?
Let’s first address an example of a typo: is anything spelled “COMMOM” instead of “COMMON”?

trees.loc[trees["common_name"].str.contains("COMMOM"), "common_name"].value_counts()


# Fix the typo, and squash any double spaces into single spaces
trees["common_name"] = (trees["common_name"]
                        .str.replace("COMMOM", "COMMON")
                        .str.replace(r"\s+", " ", regex=True))


Duplicates
Each tree has a unique ID, so duplicated() alone finds nothing. But are some trees listed twice with different IDs? Let’s compare every column except the ID.

other_cols = trees.columns.drop("tree_id")
dupes = trees.duplicated(subset=other_cols)
print("Duplicate trees:", dupes.sum())

# Example: same tree, same exact spot, two different IDs
trees[trees.duplicated(subset=other_cols, keep=False)].sort_values(["lat", "lon"]).head(4)


trees = trees[~dupes]
trees.shape

TRY IT YOURSELF (Hard): List the common names that appear only once. Can you spot any that look like mistakes (i.e., typos vs. one-offs)?

# your code here



Show solution

counts = trees["common_name"].value_counts()
counts[counts == 1]
Most are real (just rare) trees, but this is a quick way to find candidates to double-check. Real datasets almost always have a few more typos hiding somewhere!

title: How to Win a Datathon 101
text:
6. Impossible values & outliers
Additional exercises: we won’t have time for these during the workshop. Try them on your own afterwards; hints and solutions are included!
Are there any values that don’t make sense?

trees[["height_m", "diameter_cm"]].describe()

A tree with a diameter of 0 cm? And look at that max: let’s see the biggest “trees”.

print("Diameter = 0:", (trees["diameter_cm"] == 0).sum())
print("Height = 0:  ", (trees["height_m"] == 0).sum())

trees.nlargest(5, "diameter_cm")[["common_name", "height_m", "diameter_cm", "neighbourhood"]]

A pin oak that’s over 66 metres wide? That’s wider than most buildings. Definitely a data entry error!
Decision: keep trees with a height above 0 and a diameter between 0 and 500 cm. There’s no single “right” cut-off. What matters is that you choose one sensibly and explain why.

valid = (trees["height_m"] > 0) & (trees["diameter_cm"] > 0) & (trees["diameter_cm"] < 500)
print("Removing:", (~valid).sum(), "trees")

trees = trees[valid]
trees[["height_m", "diameter_cm"]].describe()

TRY IT YOURSELF (Medium): We only filtered diameter outliers. What are the 5 tallest trees left?
Hint: Use nlargest() in your solution.

# your code here



Show solution

trees.nlargest(5, "height_m")[["common_name", "height_m", "diameter_cm", "neighbourhood"]]
Three of the five tallest trees are in Kensington-Cedar Cottage, and some of them are species that are usually quite small, like the pyramidal hornbeam. Other trees like the Douglas fir are native BC trees known for growing very tall.

title: How to Win a Datathon 101
text:
7. Save our clean data
We’ll save our cleaned data in a new subfolder called processed, inside our data folder.
Why keep raw and processed data separate? - Your original data stays untouched, so you can always start over if something goes wrong. - Your team knows which file to use, so everyone works from the same clean version. - Your project stays organized as you create more files.

trees.to_csv("data/processed/trees_clean.csv", index=False)
print(f"Started with {len(trees_raw):,} rows, now {len(trees):,} clean trees.")

title: How to Win a Datathon 101
text:
Creating an EDA Chart
Every time you make a chart, walk through three quick steps: 1. What’s my question? 2. Which pointer is it? (one variable at a time? compare & connect?) 3. What kind of data? (category or number?) → which chart?

EXAMPLE: Exploring Tree Diameters

Question: How big are Vancouver’s trees? How are trunk diameters spread out?
Pointer: One variable at a time: we’re looking at a single column, diameter_cm.
Data type: diameter is a number → so we use a histogram.


ax = trees["diameter_cm"].plot(kind="hist", bins=50, color="mediumseagreen", figsize=(8, 5))
ax.set_title("How wide are Vancouver's trees?")
ax.set_xlabel("Trunk diameter (cm)")
ax.set_ylabel("Number of trees")
plt.tight_layout()
plt.show()

Most trees are on the left: about 78% are under 50 cm wide, and the typical (median) tree is about 25 cm. Then there’s a long tail of a few very big trees stretching to the right (that’s why the x-axis goes all the way out to almost 500 cm).
That shape is called right-skewed. It suggests the city has lots of young or small street trees and only a few giants. It’s also why we often use the median rather than the mean in this dataset: those few giants pull the mean up.
Notice every chart has a title and axis labels. Try to do the same in yours!
TRY IT YOURSELF (Easy): Which 5 neighbourhoods have the fewest trees? Before coding: which pointer is this, and which chart fits?
Hint: Neighbourhood is a category, and we’re counting. Filter out "Unknown" first, then use value_counts().nsmallest(5) and .plot(kind="barh").

# your code here



Show solution

known = trees[trees["neighbourhood"] != "Unknown"]
fewest = known["neighbourhood"].value_counts().nsmallest(5).sort_values(ascending=False)

ax = fewest.plot(kind="barh", color="mediumseagreen")
ax.set_title("5 neighbourhoods with the fewest trees")
ax.set_xlabel("Number of trees")
ax.set_ylabel("")
plt.tight_layout()
plt.show()
Pointer: one variable at a time (what’s rare?). Chart: bar chart, because neighbourhood is a category. Stanley Park, Strathcona, South Cambie, the West End and Fairview have the fewest trees. Many of these are smaller or denser areas, so a count doesn’t tell the whole story!

TRY IT YOURSELF (Medium): Do the 5 most common tree families (genus) differ in height? Which pointer is this, and which chart fits?
Hint: We’re comparing a number (height) across groups (genus). Keep only the top 5 genera with .isin(), then try .boxplot(column="height_m", by="genus").

# your code here



Show solution

top5 = trees["genus"].value_counts().head(5).index
subset = trees[trees["genus"].isin(top5)]

subset.boxplot(column="height_m", by="genus", figsize=(8, 5))
plt.suptitle("")   # removes an automatic extra title
plt.title("Tree height by genus (top 5)")
plt.xlabel("Genus")
plt.ylabel("Height (m)")
plt.tight_layout()
plt.show()
Pointer: compare & connect (how do groups differ?). Chart: box plot, which compares a number across groups. Oaks (QUERCUS) and lindens (TILIA) tend to be the tallest, with a median of about 14 m, while maples (ACER) and cherries/plums (PRUNUS) are the shortest at about 8 m. The dots are outliers. Why does the TILIA box look squashed flat? So many lindens are recorded at exactly 13.7 m that the box collapses: another clue that heights were recorded in ranges!

TRY IT YOURSELF (Hard): Do taller trees tend to be wider? Which pointer is this, and which chart fits?
Hint: Two numbers → scatter plot. With ~180,000 trees the dots pile up, so plot a random sample with trees.sample(2000, random_state=1) and make the dots see-through with alpha=0.3.

# your code here



Show solution

sample = trees.sample(2000, random_state=1)

ax = sample.plot(kind="scatter", x="diameter_cm", y="height_m",
                 alpha=0.3, s=10, color="mediumseagreen", figsize=(8, 5))
ax.set_title("Height vs. diameter (2,000 random trees)")
ax.set_xlabel("Trunk diameter (cm)")
ax.set_ylabel("Height (m)")
plt.tight_layout()
plt.show()
Pointer: compare & connect (do two things move together?). Chart: scatter plot, for two numbers. The dots trend upward: taller trees tend to be wider. Did you notice the dots form horizontal stripes? That’s because heights were recorded in ranges, not measured exactly. And that lonely dot up at 70 m? It’s our pyramidal hornbeam from Part 1! Surprises worth following.

title: How to Win a Datathon 101
section: EXAMPLE: Classification - Is this tree a cherry?
text:
EXAMPLE: Classification - Is this tree a cherry?

Step 1: Choose the target & features

Target (what we predict): is_cherry, True or False
Features (the clues): height_m, diameter_cm and neighbourhood

Models only understand numbers, so we turn neighbourhood into many True/False columns, one per neighbourhood. This is called one-hot encoding, and pd.get_dummies() does it for us.

# 1. Remove trees with an unknown neighbourhood
model_data = trees[trees["neighbourhood"] != "___"]

# 2. Target: what we want to predict
y = model_data["___"]

# 3. Features: the clues we'll use (one-hot encode the neighbourhood column)
X = pd.___(model_data[["___", "___", "neighbourhood"]],
           columns=["___"])

# 4. Check the result
print("Rows:", X.shape[0], " Feature columns:", X.shape[1])
X.iloc[:3, :6]



Step 2: Split the data
We keep 20% of trees hidden as a test set. The model learns from the other 80%, then we check how well it does on trees it has never seen, like studying with practice questions and then writing the real exam.

X_train, X_test, y_train, y_test = train_test_split(
    ..., ..., test_size=..., random_state=42)

print("Training trees:", len(X_train))
print("Test trees:    ", len(X_test))
print("Cherries in the test set:", y_test.sum())



Step 3: Start with a baseline
DUMMY MODEL - the simplest possible model: always guess the most common answer, which is not a cherry.
We’ll check two scores for every model (plus how long it takes to train): - Accuracy: what % of all trees did we label correctly? - Recall: of the real cherries, what % did we find?
This small helper function trains a model and adds its scores to a results table, so we don’t repeat the same code for every model.

results = []   # tip: re-run this cell to clear the table if you get duplicate rows

def evaluate(name, model):
    start = time.time()
    model.fit(X_train, y_train)            # learn from the training data
    seconds = time.time() - start
    predictions = model.predict(X_test)    # predict on unseen trees
    results.append({
        "model": name,
        "accuracy_%": round(accuracy_score(y_test, predictions) * 100, 1),
        "recall_%": round(recall_score(y_test, predictions) * 100, 1),
        "train_seconds": round(seconds, 2),
    })
    return pd.DataFrame(results)

evaluate("Baseline: always 'not a cherry'", DummyClassifier(strategy="most_frequent"))

About 90% accurate… but 0% recall! Because only ~10% of trees are cherries, a model that never says “cherry” is still right 90% of the time.
Lesson: accuracy can be very misleading when the thing you’re looking for is rare. Always compare against a baseline!


Step 4: Train & compare models
Let’s try two common beginner-friendly models: - Logistic regression: draws a boundary between “cherry” and “not cherry” (despite the name, it’s for classification!) - Decision tree: learns a series of yes/no questions, like a flowchart. max_depth=5 limits it to 5 questions deep so it doesn’t memorize the training data.

evaluate("Logistic regression", LogisticRegression(max_iter=1000))
evaluate("Decision tree", DecisionTreeClassifier(max_depth=5, random_state=42))

Both models beat the baseline’s accuracy, but only by a little, and they still miss most of the cherries.


Step 5: Evaluate: what does our client care about?
If the City wants to find blossom spots, missing cherries is worse than a few false alarms. We can tell the model that cherries matter more with class_weight="balanced".

tree_balanced = DecisionTreeClassifier(max_depth=5, random_state=42, class_weight="balanced")
evaluate("Decision tree (cherries matter more)", tree_balanced)

The trade-off: accuracy drops to about 84%, but now we catch about 62% of the cherries, up from 24%. Which model is “best” depends on what your client cares about. That’s a decision worth explaining to the judges!
A model is only as good as its features. With only size and location, there’s a limit to how well we can spot cherries. If we had flower colour or bloom time, it would do much better.
Lesson: more complex doesn’t always mean more accurate. A slightly better score isn’t always worth losing the ability to explain your model.


3. Match the model to your question
There’s no single “best” model; it depends on what your client needs. For example:








If your client wants to…
A good choice might be…
Because…




Understand why (explain to the City)
A small decision tree or logistic regression
Easy to read and explain


Catch as many cherries as possible
A model with class_weight="balanced"
It focuses on the rare group


Squeeze out the best score (e.g. a leaderboard)
Random forest or gradient boosting
Often a bit more accurate, if you have time



For our client (the City promoting blossom spots), we’d probably pick the simple balanced decision tree: it catches most cherries and we can explain how it works.

title: About
text:
I graduated with my BSc in Cognitive Systems with a Minor in Data Science from UBC. Throughout my undergrad I worked in multiple research labs across UBC, where I gained experience applying data-driven approaches to investigate questions in social psychology, cognitive science, and sports biomechanics.
In the summer of 2025, I was selected as one of eight individuals for the UBC Data Science Institute’s Data Science for Social Good (DSSG) Program. We partnered with Mentor Canada, the largest non-profit dedicated to expanding access to youth mentorship nationally, to support an upcoming grant application by analyzing survey data to better understand the current landscape of youth mentorship in Canada. Alongside this analysis, I independently designed and implemented a retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) system to streamline Mentor Canada’s research workflow, enabling the organization to more efficiently access insights from their existing documents.
Following my undergraduate studies, I joined MNP as a Data Analyst in Human Capital. My work involved developing reports and dashboards, analyzing workforce data, and finding ways to improve data usage and management. Moving into industry gave me a new perspective on working with data and helped me understand how analysis can be translated into meaningful insights for organizational decision-making.
Currently, I am completing my Master of Data Science at UBC where I am expanding my technical foundation and broadening my experience across different areas of data science.

title: Python: Visualizing the palmerpenguins Dataset
text:
Data: Palmer Penguins, Palmer Station Antarctica LTER.

import pandas as pd
import seaborn as sns
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
from palmerpenguins import load_penguins


penguins = load_penguins()

missing_values = (
    penguins.isna()
    .sum()
    .reset_index()
    .rename(columns={"index": "variable", 0: "n_missing"})
)

print(missing_values)

            variable  n_missing
0            species          0
1             island          0
2     bill_length_mm          2
3      bill_depth_mm          2
4  flipper_length_mm          2
5        body_mass_g          2
6                sex         11
7               year          0


Before doing any exploratory data analysis, I loaded in the tidyverse and palmerpenguins libraries. I then created a tibble showing the number of missing values in each column of the penguins dataset. I thought that checking for missing data would help identify any gaps in the data can quietly affect summaries and plots later on. For the most part, columns had non-NA values but sex has 11 missing values, and there are 2 penguins that are missing all of their body measurements. Because of this, I use drop_na() in later steps to remove incomplete rows before calculating averages.

missing_sex = (
    penguins.assign(missing=penguins["sex"].isna())
    .groupby(["species", "missing"], observed=True)
    .size()
    .reset_index(name="n")
)
missing_sex["total"] = missing_sex.groupby("species", observed=True)["n"].transform("sum")
missing_sex["percent"] = (missing_sex["n"] / missing_sex["total"] * 100).round(1)
missing_sex = missing_sex[missing_sex["missing"]]

missing_sex

I wanted to understand which penguin species were missing values for sex and how much of the data was missing relative to each species. The Adelie species is missing 6 records, accounting for 3.9% of Adelie penguins, while Gentoo is missing 5, accounting for 4.0% of Gentoo penguins. Although Adelie has more missing records, the proportions are nearly identical because Adelie has more penguins overall. Chinstrap does not appear in the missing_sex tibble, which indicates that no Chinstrap records are missing sex. Overall, only 11 of 344 penguins (about 3.2%) are missing sex, so the missing values are unlikely to have a large effect on comparisons between males and females.

mean_bill_length_mm = (
    penguins.dropna()
    .groupby(["species", "sex"], observed=True, as_index=False)["bill_length_mm"]
    .mean()
    .rename(columns={"bill_length_mm": "average_bill_length"})
)


sns.barplot(
    data=mean_bill_length_mm,
    x="species",
    y="average_bill_length",
    hue="sex"
)
plt.title("Average bill length by species and sex")
plt.xlabel("Species")
plt.ylabel("Average bill length (mm)")
plt.legend(title="Sex")
plt.show()







Figure 1: Average Bill Length by Sex and Species





After visualizing the average bill_length_mm by species and sex, we can see that for all three species (Adelie, Chinstrap, and Gentoo), the average bill length of female penguins is consistently shorter than that of male penguins. In addition, Adelie penguins have the shortest bills overall, while Chinstrap and Gentoo penguins have comparable average bill lengths when accounting for sex.

Even in the short amount of time I have been in the program, I can see that immersion and consistency will play a large role in success. The different ways of exposure to new material allows us to both solidfy our understand and identify areas of improvement from various angles.

title: R: Visualizing the palmerpenguins Dataset
text:
Data: Palmer Penguins, Palmer Station Antarctica LTER.

library(tidyverse)
library(palmerpenguins)


missing_values <- penguins |>
  summarise(across(everything(), ~ sum(is.na(.x)))) |>
  pivot_longer(everything(), names_to = "variable", values_to = "n_missing")

missing_values

# A tibble: 8 × 2
  variable          n_missing
  <chr>                 <int>
1 species                   0
2 island                    0
3 bill_length_mm            2
4 bill_depth_mm             2
5 flipper_length_mm         2
6 body_mass_g               2
7 sex                      11
8 year                      0


Before doing any exploratory data analysis, I loaded in the tidyverse and palmerpenguins libraries. I then created a tibble showing the number of missing values in each column of the penguins dataset. I thought that checking for missing data would help identify any gaps in the data can quietly affect summaries and plots later on. For the most part, columns had non-NA values but sex has 11 missing values, and there are 2 penguins that are missing all of their body measurements. Because of this, I use drop_na() in later steps to remove incomplete rows before calculating averages.

missing_sex <- penguins |>
  count(species, missing = is.na(sex)) |>
  group_by(species) |>
  mutate(total = sum(n),
         percent = round(n / sum(n) * 100, 1)) |>
  ungroup() |>
  filter(missing)     

missing_sex

# A tibble: 2 × 5
  species missing     n total percent
  <fct>   <lgl>   <int> <int>   <dbl>
1 Adelie  TRUE        6   152     3.9
2 Gentoo  TRUE        5   124     4  


I wanted to understand which penguin species were missing values for sex and how much of the data was missing relative to each species. The Adelie species is missing 6 records, accounting for 3.9% of Adelie penguins, while Gentoo is missing 5, accounting for 4.0% of Gentoo penguins. Although Adelie has more missing records, the proportions are nearly identical because Adelie has more penguins overall. Chinstrap does not appear in the missing_sex tibble, which indicates that no Chinstrap records are missing sex. Overall, only 11 of 344 penguins (about 3.2%) are missing sex, so the missing values are unlikely to have a large effect on comparisons between males and females.

mean_bill_length_mm <- penguins |>
    drop_na() |>
  group_by(species, sex) |>
  summarise(average_bill_length = mean(bill_length_mm))


mean_bill_length_mm |>
  ggplot(aes(x = species, y = average_bill_length, fill = sex)) +
  geom_col(position = "dodge") +
  labs(
    title = "Average bill length by species and sex",
    x = "Species",
    y = "Average bill length (mm)",
    fill = "Sex"
  )







Figure 1: Average Bill Length by Sex and Species





After visualizing the average bill_length_mm by species and sex, we can see that for all three species (Adelie, Chinstrap, and Gentoo), the average bill length of female penguins is consistently shorter than that of male penguins. In addition, Adelie penguins have the shortest bills overall, while Chinstrap and Gentoo penguins have comparable average bill lengths when accounting for sex.

title: How to Win a Datathon 101
text:
I designed and led How to Win a Datathon 101, a hands-on workshop for Dataverse 2026. The goal was to give beginners a repeatable workflow they could take straight into a datathon: meet your data, explore it with purpose, model only the insights that you can explain, and tell a story the judges will remember.
Participants worked through a Jupyter notebook alongside the slides, with TRY IT YOURSELF! exercises at three levels (Easy, Medium, Hard) and hidden solutions to check their work.

title: How to Win a Datathon 101
text:
The case

The (hypothetical) client: the City of Vancouver wants to run a campaign that gets residents and visitors exploring more neighbourhoods, driving foot traffic to local businesses. They want to know which areas to promote, and when.

The data: the City of Vancouver’s Public trees dataset, with ~184,000 trees (Open Government Licence – Vancouver).

title: How to Win a Datathon 101
text:
What we covered
Part 1: Meet & clean your data. Six checks to run on any new dataset: structure, relevant variables, missing values, data types, inconsistencies, and impossible values & outliers. One highlight: about 3,900 trees had no neighbourhood, and most of them turned out to be in Stanley Park. If we had preemptively deleted them, we would have lost data for one of Vancouver’s most famous parks.
Part 2: Exploratory data analysis. Four pointers for EDA (i.e., start with a question, one variable at a time, compare & connect, follow the surprises) and how the kind of question you ask points you to the right chart.
Part 3: Data modelling. A full classification walkthrough: can we predict whether a tree is a cherry from its size and neighbourhood? We compared a baseline against logistic regression and a decision tree, and saw why accuracy can be misleading when the thing you’re looking for is rare. A dummy model that never says “cherry” is still ~90% accurate! Weighting the rare class brought recall from ~24% to ~62%.
Top secret: a blueprint for a winning project. Strong technical work is the foundation, but winning projects also have impact and tell a story.

title: How to Win a Datathon 101
text:
Key takeaways

Look before you clean. Understand your data’s condition and limits before changing anything.
Every fix is a decision. Be able to explain your choices, and write them down as you go.
Don’t delete blindly. Missing or odd data might be telling you something more than what’s on the surface.
Start simple. Begin with a baseline, pick the score that matters to your client, and only add complexity if it clearly helps.


Slides


Tools: Python, pandas, matplotlib, scikit-learn, Jupyter / Google Colab

title: Exploring the Impact of Youth Mentorship
text:
Overview
After the completion of my undergraduate degree, I spent the summer as a Data Science for Social Good Fellow at the UBC Data Science Institute. With my teammates Isobel Adams and Vincy Huang, I partnered with Mentor Canada, a national nonprofit working to expand access to quality mentorship and reduce gaps in who gets a mentor.
Mentor Canada relies heavily on grant funding, so our goal was to strengthen the evidence base for their grant applications using clear data-driven insights.

title: Exploring the Impact of Youth Mentorship
text:
The question

How does mentorship shape long-term life outcomes for youth, especially those from underserved communities?

The data: Mentor Canada’s national Mapping the Mentoring Gap survey, with 2,838 responses from young adults aged 18–30. It covers their current life outcomes (income, education, mental health) and looks back at their childhood: socioeconomic background, whether they had a mentor between ages 6 and 18, the quality of that mentorship, and the barriers they faced.

title: Exploring the Impact of Youth Mentorship
text:
What we did
Cleaning a 700+ column survey. We took the raw survey from 737 columns down to a clean, analysis-ready dataset (n = 2,396) in R: standardizing responses, handling ambiguous answers like “Unsure”, reverse-coding Likert scales, and comparing imputation approaches (mean-mode with tidymodels and k-NN with FAISS).
Statistical modelling. We used logistic, ordinal logistic and linear regression, permutation-based ANOVA, and specification curve analysis to check how robust our findings were.
Finding subgroups. Latent Class Analysis (LCA) revealed three groups of youth, from highest- to lowest-performing across employment, education, mental health, belonging and social support. We also explored autoencoder-based clustering.
A RAG chatbot for grant writing. We built a Retrieval-Augmented Generation system grounded in Mentor Canada’s own reports, so their team can quickly pull evidence when writing grants. It uses an OCR pipeline (pytesseract), LangChain, mxbai-embed-large embeddings, a Pinecone vector store and the open-source Mistral model, evaluated with an LLM-as-a-judge approach (average faithfulness 0.95, answer relevancy 0.86).

title: Exploring the Impact of Youth Mentorship
text:
Key findings

Mentorship boosts education. For youth from low-SES backgrounds, having a mentor was linked to a 10% higher high school graduation rate. Mentorship also helped low-SES youth more than high-SES youth in pursuing further education.
Mentorship helps close the income gap. The median income gap between high- and low-SES youth was about $13,600 without a mentor, compared with about $7,200 with one.
Mentorship supports mental health. Youth with a mentor reported better mental health. Formal mentorship was linked to 2.6× higher odds of reporting good mental health.
Barriers aren’t felt equally. 63% of low-SES youth reported unmet mentoring needs, compared with 46% of high-SES youth. Low-SES youth were also more likely to be waitlisted for a program.

These are associations, not proof of cause and effect, and they come from a single survey. Still, together they make a strong case for making mentorship more accessible, especially for underserved youth.

title: Exploring the Impact of Youth Mentorship
text:
My role

Statistical modelling. I ran regression models (logistic, ordinal logistic and linear) to find what predicts youth outcomes such as further education, unmet mentoring needs and mental health, and to test whether mentorship narrows the gap between low- and high-SES youth.
Built the RAG chatbot. I worked on the full pipeline: turning Mentor Canada’s scanned PDFs into searchable text with OCR, splitting it into chunks, creating embeddings, storing them in a Pinecone vector database, and generating answers with the open-source Mistral model. I also designed the prompts to keep answers grounded in Mentor Canada’s own sources.
Evaluated the chatbot. I helped set up an LLM-as-a-judge evaluation to check that answers were faithful to the sources and relevant to the question, and to make the test questions more realistic.

Tools: R (tidyverse, tidymodels, poLCA), Python (statsmodels, PyTorch, FAISS), LangChain, Pinecone, Mistral
